If this object is replaced with an object of mass $2m$ (the lengths of the springs do not change, and both springs are within the elastic limit), when the object is again in equilibrium, the object has descended by $x$ compared with its position at the first equilibrium. ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure as a whole is very dark; only a cyan object block can be recognized, and inside the block is marked “2m”. The specific shapes of the springs, the fixed points P/Q, and the position labels of k1 and k2 in the figure cannot be clearly verified, so these details are not taken as facts directly obtained from image observation. Reasoning: The following sets up equations according to the upper and lower two-spring vertical connection model referred to by “as shown in the figure” in the problem statement; to avoid relying on indistinguishable numbering positions, let the stiffness coefficients of the upper and lower springs be ku and kd respectively. They are some correspondence of k1 and k2, so ku+kd=k1+k2. At the first equilibrium, the object of mass m is subject to gravity mg. The problem statement says that the upper spring is in its original-length state, so the elastic force of the upper spring is 0. Let the upward elastic force exerted by the lower spring on the object at this time be Fd; then equilibrium gives Fd=mg. After replacing it with an object of mass 2m, the object descends by x compared with the first equilibrium position. Under this upper-and-lower spring model, the upper spring changes by x relative to its original length, producing an upward restoring force ku x; the lower spring is compressed by an additional x relative to the first equilibrium, so the upward elastic force increases by kd x and becomes Fd+kd x. At the second equilibrium, the sum of the upward elastic forces equals the gravity 2mg: Fd+kd x+ku x=2mg. Substituting Fd=mg gives mg+(ku+kd)x=2mg, so (ku+kd)x=mg. Also ku+kd=k1+k2, hence x=mg/(k1+k2).
